blocks.text: Outside the biblical narrative, Jehu appears in Assyrian records as a tributary king submitting to Shalmaneser III. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III, erected at the palace complex of Kalhu/Nimrud, depicts labeled reliefs of subject peoples. One register presents 'Iaua, son of Omri' in Levantine dress, prostrating before the Assyrian king with tribute bearers presenting luxury goods. This inscription dates to Shalmaneser III's 18th regnal year, shortly after the biblical chronology places Jehu's coup. The obelisk supplies near-contemporary, external corroboration that Jehu ruled and submitted to Assyrian dominion, though it does not detail the coup narrative itself.
